title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 27
paragraphs: On the twenty-fifth of August, so his historians tell us, Napoleon spent the entire day on horseback, inspecting the terrain, considering plans submitted by his marshals, and personally giving orders to his generals.

The original Russian line along the river Kolocha had been disrupted by the capture of the Shevardino Redoubt on the twenty-fourth, and part of the line—the left flank—had been pulled back. That part was not entrenched, and in front of it the ground was more open and level than elsewhere. It was obvious to anyone, military or civilian, that this was where the French should attack. It would seem that no great deliberation was needed to reach this conclusion, nor any special effort on the part of the Emperor and his marshals, nor any need for that supreme quality called genius which people are so ready to attribute to Napoleon; yet the historians who described the event later, and the men who surrounded Napoleon at the time, and Napoleon himself, all thought otherwise.

Napoleon rode across the plain, surveyed the terrain with a profound air and in silence, nodded approvingly or shook his head dubiously, and without explaining to the generals around him the deep course of reasoning behind his decisions, merely gave them his final conclusions as commands. Having heard a suggestion from Davout (now called the Prince of Eckmuhl) to turn the Russian left wing, Napoleon said it should not be done, without explaining why. To a proposal by General Campan (who was to attack the fleches) to lead his division through the woods, Napoleon agreed, though the so-called Duke of Elchingen (Ney) ventured to remark that a move through the woods was dangerous and might throw the division into disorder.

After inspecting the terrain opposite the Shevardino Redoubt, Napoleon pondered briefly in silence and then indicated where two batteries should be placed by the next morning to act against the Russian entrenchments, and where the field artillery should be positioned in line with them.
After giving these and other orders, he returned to his tent, and the battle plan was written down from his dictation.
These dispositions, which French historians write about with enthusiasm and other historians with deep respect, were as follows:
At dawn the two new batteries established during the night on the plain occupied by the Prince of Eckmuhl will open fire on the opposing batteries of the enemy.

At the same time the commander of the artillery of the 1st Corps, General Pernetti, with thirty cannon of Campan's division and all the howitzers of Dessaix's and Friant's divisions, will move forward, open fire, and bombard the enemy's battery, against which will operate:
24 guns of the Guard artillery, 30 guns of Campan's division,
and 8 guns of Friant's and Dessaix's divisions—
in all 62 guns.

The commander of the artillery of the 3rd Corps, General Fouche, will place the howitzers of the 3rd and 8th Corps, sixteen in all, on the flanks of the battery that is to bombard the entrenchment on the left, which will have forty guns in all directed against it.
General Sorbier must be ready at the first order to advance with all the howitzers of the Guard artillery against either entrenchment.
During the cannonade, Prince Poniatowski is to advance through the wood on the village and turn the enemy's position.
General Campan will move through the wood to seize the first fortification.
After the advance has begun in this manner, orders will be given in accordance with the enemy's movements.

The cannonade on the left flank will begin as soon as the guns on the right wing are heard. The sharpshooters of Morand's division and of the Viceroy's division will open heavy fire when they see the attack begin on the right wing.

The Viceroy will occupy the village and cross by its three bridges, advancing to the same heights as Morand's and Gerard's divisions, which under his command will be directed against the redoubt and fall into line with the rest of the forces.
All this must be done in good order, retaining troops in reserve as far as possible.
The Imperial Camp near Mozhaysk,
September 6, 1812.

These dispositions, which are very vague and confused if one allows oneself to regard the arrangements without religious awe of Napoleon's genius, consisted of four directives—four different orders. Not one of them was, or could be, carried out.

The dispositions say first that the batteries placed at the spot Napoleon chose, together with Pernetti's and Fouche's guns (102 in all), were to open fire and bombard the Russian fleches and redoubts. This could not be done, because from the spots Napoleon selected, the shells could not reach the Russian works, and those 102 guns fired into the air until the nearest commander, contrary to Napoleon's instructions, moved them forward.

The second order was that Poniatowski, advancing on the village through the wood, should turn the Russian left flank. This could not be done and was not done, because Poniatowski, advancing through the wood, met Tuchkov there blocking his way, and could not and did not turn the Russian position.

The third order was: General Campan will move through the wood to seize the first fortification. Campan's division did not seize the first fortification but was driven back, because on emerging from the wood it had to re-form under grapeshot—something Napoleon hadn't foreseen.

The fourth order was: The Viceroy will occupy the village (Borodino) and cross by its three bridges, advancing to the same heights as Morand's and Gerard's divisions (for whose movements no directions are given), which under his command will be directed against the redoubt and fall into line with the rest of the forces.

As far as one can make out—not so much from this unintelligible sentence as from the Viceroy's attempts to execute it—he was to advance from the left through Borodino to the redoubt while Morand's and Gerard's divisions advanced simultaneously from the front.

All of this, like the rest of the plan, was not and could not be executed. After passing through Borodino, the Viceroy was driven back to the Kolocha and could get no farther; while Morand's and Gerard's divisions did not take the redoubt but were beaten back, and the redoubt was only captured at the end of the battle by cavalry (something probably unforeseen and unheard of by Napoleon). So not a single order in the plan was, or could be, carried out. But the dispositions state that after the fight begins in this manner, orders will be given according to the enemy's movements—and so it might be supposed that Napoleon would make all necessary adjustments during the battle. But this was not and could not be done, because throughout the entire battle Napoleon was so far away that (as later became clear) he could not follow the battle's progress, and not one of his orders during the fight could be carried out.
